title: Tripartite entanglement of remote atomic qubits
authors: Isabella Goetting, Ashish Kalakuntla, Mikhail Shalaev, Harriet Bufan Shi, Ana Ferrari, Sagnik Saha, George Toh, Saki Male, Christopher Monroe
abstract: Distributed entanglement across multi-node quantum networks is essential for a wide range of quantum technologies, including modular quantum computers, distributed sensing and metrology, and multi-party secure communication protocols. Such large-scale quantum networks will require photonic interconnects to generate and sustain entangled states across localized nodes. Previously, three-node distributed Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states have been generated between solid-state qubits and atomic ensembles, but not yet in the platform of individual atomic qubits, which can be replicated, detected, and individually controlled with high fidelity. Here we report the first fully-distributed GHZ state of qubits across a three-node quantum network of single atomic memories, using photonic interconnects. We achieve a bounded fidelity of $0.841(17) \leq \mathcal{F} \leq 0.881(17)$ at an entanglement generation rate of 0.095(5)/sec and measure a clear violation of Mermin's inequality while closing the detection loophole for the first time in a fully-distributed multipartite entangled state.
summary: The research successfully generated the first fully-distributed GHZ state involving single atomic qubits across three remote nodes. This was achieved by coupling trapped ions to photons and interfering these photons at an external generator. The results confirm multipartite entanglement via Mermin's inequality violation, advancing the feasibility of large-scale quantum networks.
main_problem: The primary goal was to generate and demonstrate fully-distributed Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states of qubits across a three-node quantum network using photonic interconnects.
main_result: The authors reported the first such demonstration, achieving a bounded fidelity between 0.841 and 0.881 and closing the detection loophole for the first time in this fully-distributed multipartite entangled state.
method: Entanglement was generated by coupling single trapped ion qubits to emitted photons, which were then sent through optical fibers to an external GHZ-state generator where they interfered.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a three-node quantum network composed of spatially separated trapped ions ($^{138}	ext{Ba}^+$). Entanglement is mediated by single photons collected from spontaneous emission and interfering at a central optical setup.
key_observables: GHZ State Fidelity (F), violation of Mermin's inequality, entanglement generation rate, and pairwise visibilities.
important_parameters: Fidelity bounds ($0.841 \le F \le 0.881$), entanglement rate ($\sim 0.095/	ext{sec}$), and the classical bound violation for Mermin's parameter ($M > 2$).
main_assumptions: The fidelity analysis relies on bounding techniques using measured populations and parity contrasts, while error sources include photonic spatial mode mismatch and polarization mixing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the three ion trap nodes and the GHZ generator setup; subsequent figures detail state characterization via parity fringes and correlator measurements used to quantify entanglement violation.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, describes the process of generating single-photon entangled states between ions and photons, outlines the interference mechanism at the GHZ generator, and finally presents quantitative results on fidelity bounding and Mermin inequality violation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses scalability in quantum networking by demonstrating multipartite entanglement across physically separated nodes using photonic links, which is a cornerstone challenge for distributed quantum computation.
